answer.answer: The earliest arrival time at T is 4. The tie-broken route is S wait A T.

claims.quote: The earliest arrival time at T is 4.
The tie-broken route is S wait A T.

derivation_steps.statement: For an edge (u,v;base,penalty), departing at integer time t costs base+penalty*(t mod 2), and arrival parity is t parity plus the cost parity.
At S time 0 (even), S-A costs 1 and reaches A at time 1 (odd); S-B costs 3 and reaches B at time 3 (odd).
At A time 1 (odd), A-T costs 2+6*1=8, reaching T at 9; waiting one unit reaches A time 2 (even).
At A time 2 (even), A-T costs 2+6*0=2, reaching T at 4.
Waiting at S from time 0 to 1, then S-A costs 1 and reaches A at time 2 (even), then A-T costs 2 and reaches T at 4.

No route reaches T before 4: via A the earliest even departure is time 2 and A-T costs 2, so T is at least 4; B is first reached at time 3 (odd), and even the fastest B-to-T continuation (wait to B even time 4, B-A costs 2 to A time 6, then A-T costs 2) reaches T at 8; C is first reached at time 5 (odd) and C-T costs 4 to T at 9; D first reached at time 6 (even) and D-T costs 3 to T at 9. Thus T cannot be reached before 4.
Therefore the earliest arrival time at T is 4.
The two routes achieving arrival 4 are S wait A T (wait at S, then S-A, then A-T) and S A wait T (S-A, wait at A, then A-T).
Under the tie-break rule that lexicographically orders token `wait` before vertex names, S wait A T is smaller than S A wait T because after common S the next token is wait versus A.
Hence the tie-broken route is S wait A T.
